title: Request-Response Patterns
description: Learn request/response, one-way, and fire-and-forget patterns for service communication.

data.text: Different interaction patterns suit different scenarios. Request-response is the most common, but one-way and fire-and-forget patterns are essential for performance and reliability.

terms.definition: The caller sends a request and waits for a response.
The caller sends a request and does not wait for a response.
The caller sends a message and does not care about the result.
A pattern where the responder notifies the caller when done.

items: Used for queries and commands needing confirmation

data.text: Use request-response when you need a result. Use one-way when you need notification but not a result. Use fire-and-forget when the result does not matter, like logging.

data.title: Exercise: Choose Interaction Patterns
data.description: Choose the right pattern for each scenario.
steps: Order placed: needs confirmation but can be async
Audit log: does not need confirmation
Email notification: needs delivery but not response
Analytics event: does not need confirmation
data.expectedOutcome: A table mapping scenarios to patterns with justifications

items.question: What is the difference between one-way and fire-and-forget?
items.answer: One-way usually has delivery guarantees (broker ack). Fire-and-forget has no guarantees.

items.question: When should I avoid request-response?
items.answer: When the operation is long-running or when you need high throughput. Use async patterns instead.

items.question: Can I combine patterns?
items.answer: Yes. Use request-response for the initial request and async callbacks for long-running work.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Request-response for results, one-way for notifications, fire-and-forget for non-critical
Blocking patterns are simpler but limit throughput
Choose based on whether you need a result
data.takeaway: Match the interaction pattern to the reliability and latency requirements.
